item.title: Weighted Point Cloud Normal Estimation
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners carry no normals and are often corrupted by noise, yet accurate normals help downstream tasks such as noise filtering and surface reconstruction. The classic approach, PCA, computes each point’s normal from the covariance of its neighbours; it is simple but tends to blur details and is fragile on noisy data. Learning-based regressors such as PCPNet and Nesti-Net are more robust to noise, but they ignore that neighbouring points contribute differently to the central point’s normal, which can make them inaccurate on complex surfaces. Surface-fitting methods such as DeepFit and AdaFit adapt well to complicated geometry but become less robust under severe noise.

How it works

The method regresses the normal of each point from a local patch around it, and it learns to weight the points of that patch by how relevant they are to the central point. Training has two stages: a contrastive pre-training stage that teaches the point encoder and weight regressor to relate patches to normals, and a normal estimation stage that fine-tunes them together with a normal regressor.

  1. A local patch. For each point, the patch contains its N nearest neighbours (N = 700 in the experiments). The patch is normalised to a unit sphere and aligned with a rotation R computed by PCA on the patch.
  2. Uniform weights fall short. Regressing the normal with every point weighted equally lets less relevant neighbours pull the estimate away from the true normal.
  3. Learned point weights. A point encoder built from DGCNN’s EdgeConv layers produces per-point features, and an MLP weight regressor predicts a weight for each point. The training target is the squared cosine between the central point’s ground-truth normal and each neighbour’s ground-truth normal, so points with similar normals count as more relevant. The weights multiply the features element-wise, F′ = W ⊙ F.
  4. Contrastive pre-training. A second branch encodes the central point’s ground-truth normal with MLPs. Both features pass through projection heads, and a temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss pulls each patch–normal pair together while pushing apart the other pairs in the batch. The weight loss is added to this loss.
  5. Weighted normal regression. The pre-trained encoder and weight regressor are fine-tuned with a normal regressor of fully connected layers, trained with a cosine loss plus the weight loss. The predicted normal is normalised and rotated back with R⁻¹.

Results

Average RMSE 17.42° over the four noise levels of the PCPNet shapes with Gaussian noise, the lowest of all compared methods (AdaFit 17.66°, DeepFit 18.14°, best PCA setting 20.23°) (Table I).
Lowest error at the 0.60 %, 0.84 % and 1.20 % noise levels, e.g. 21.48° vs 21.94° for AdaFit at 1.20 % (Table I).
On the PCPNet validation set, the full pipeline reaches 14.46°, against 21.15° for the baseline trained with the cosine loss alone (Table II).

The synthetic test set contains 19 PCPNet shapes, each with four Gaussian noise levels (0.36 %, 0.6 %, 0.84 % and 1.2 % of the bounding-box diagonal); the method is compared with PCA, the surface-fitting methods DI, DeepFit and AdaFit, and the regression methods PCPNet and Nesti-Net. At the lowest noise level DeepFit is slightly ahead (13.18° vs 13.25°); the method’s advantage appears as the noise grows. The ablation shows that both ideas matter: without the weight regression the error is 14.70°, and without the contrastive pre-training it is 18.21°.

On raw scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, compared against the clean normals the dataset provides, the method has lower error than AdaFit and Nesti-Net on the three shapes shown. On the Paris-rue-Madame street scans, where no ground truth exists, its normals are tidier on complex areas such as a window lattice while keeping features such as a building eave and a car light. Used as input to point cloud filtering, its normals give the best filtering result by Chamfer distance, and in Poisson reconstruction of a sharp Star shape they give a more accurate tip.

item.title: Iteratively weighted principal component analysis and orientation consistency for normal estimation in point cloud
item.description:
The problem

A point cloud is only a set of 3D coordinates. Many later steps, such as denoising, segmentation, surface reconstruction and visualisation, also need a surface normal at every point, so normal estimation is a basic operation in point cloud processing. The classical method, by Hoppe et al., fits a plane to each point’s nearest neighbours with principal component analysis (PCA) and takes the plane’s normal. It assumes the neighbourhood is close to a plane, and it does not perform well where points are sparse or where the surface has sharp edges: for example, normals can turn gradually around a right angle instead of following the true edge (Fig. 2).

Where point density varies and sharp features occur, the normal directions of adjacent points can also be inconsistent, some pointing inside and some outside. Reconstruction methods such as ball-pivoting and Poisson need consistently oriented normals. Wrong normals at sharp features blur those features after reconstruction, and inconsistent orientations can break the reconstructed surface.

How it works

The method keeps PCA plane fitting as its core and adds two things around it. To make the normals more robust and reliable, it weights every neighbour by distance and by normal similarity and repeats the weighted fit a few times; the authors call this Iteratively Weighted PCA (IWPCA). To make the orientation consistent, it first flips normals using the centre of the cloud and then propagates orientation along a minimal spanning tree (MST).

  1. Local plane fit. A Kd-tree finds the k nearest neighbours of each point, and a least-squares plane is fitted to them. The normal is the eigenvector belonging to the smallest eigenvalue of the neighbourhood covariance matrix.
  2. Bilateral weights. IWPCA centres the covariance matrix on the point itself and weights each neighbour twice. The spatial weight decreases with the neighbour’s distance from the point, controlled by σd, usually half the kNN search radius. The normal weight decreases as the neighbour’s normal departs from the point’s normal, controlled by σn, usually 15° to 30°. In the first pass both normals are set to the default (1, 0, 0).
  3. Iterate. Each new pass uses the normals of the previous pass in the normal weight. More iterations give a better estimate but cost more time; the authors recommend 2 or 3, and the last pass is the result.
  4. Pre-flip towards the outside. The centre of the whole cloud is computed, and every normal that points towards it is flipped.
  5. Propagate along a minimal spanning tree. Prim’s algorithm builds an MST over neighbouring points, with edge weight 1 − |ni · nj|. Starting from the root, each child’s normal is flipped when its dot product with its parent’s normal is negative.

For sharp parts, the normals can additionally be smoothed with the same spatial and normal weights (bilateral weighted smoothing). In the authors’ tests this made the normals on sharp parts more robust but lowered their reliability, so they recommend it only when needed, since IWPCA already improves robustness at edges by itself.

Results

Four test models from the Stanford Computer Graphics Lab: Stanford bunny (34,835 points), cube (39,846), sharp cone (50,000) and a scanned surface (30,443), all with σn = 30° and σd = 0.5 (Table 1).
Stanford bunny runtime: 564 ms for PCA, 697 ms for one IWPCA iteration, 896 ms for three (Table 1).
2 or 3 iterations recommended (Section 4.1).

The comparisons in the paper are visual. On the cube, IWPCA improves the robustness of the normals at the sharp edges, and after the MST re-orientation the reliability, robustness and orientation consistency of all normals improve and the shape of the cube is clearer (Fig. 7). When the cube is reconstructed with the Poisson method, the edges and corners obtained from IWPCA normals are sharper and clearer than those from classical PCA normals (Fig. 8). On the sharp cone, classical PCA gives unsatisfactory normals at the tip, leaves some normals uncomputed and points many bottom normals inward; IWPCA improves robustness at both the top and the bottom (Fig. 9). On the scanned surface, the improved MST turns inconsistent normals so that the vast majority point to the raised side (Fig. 11).

IWPCA costs more computation than classical PCA, and its runtimes include the normal re-orientation. With one iteration it is slower than PCA; with three iterations it is somewhat faster than running classical PCA three times. The experiments ran on Windows 7 (64-bit) with an Intel Core i7-5650U CPU at 2.20 GHz and 8 GB RAM. The neighbourhood size k and the weight parameters σd and σn are hard to determine and were chosen from experience; the authors suggest deriving them from local curvature, noise distribution and point density in future work.
